rationale: A wins because it understands the real story is not robot-salad theater; it is economics, and it forces the proof before letting the founder strut. "Sweetgreen says its robot-assembled stores run higher margins than human-run ones" is the cleanest reporter-shaped hook here, with the right follow-up: margin definition, capex, throughput, and sample size. B's "Sweetgreen makes robot-assembled bowls the default, not the pilot, for new stores" is useful, but it leans on an unsupported before/after and its labor line "reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" turns a concern into a fact. Good set, just looser with the facts.
gaps_in_A: "human-run ones" is punchier than it is precise. The update says traditional stores, not necessarily purely human-run stores.

"A still-unprofitable public chain is betting the path to profit runs through automation" slightly hardens an inference into intent. The facts support the question; they do not prove management has named automation as the path to net profitability.
A mostly skips the clean rollout/adoption story around "most new stores" and retrofits. It folds that into other angles instead of giving trade ops a standalone buildout hook.
gaps_in_B: "default, not the pilot" is a smart frame, but the update never says Infinite Kitchen was a pilot. Do not invent the before-state because the headline wants a little swagger.
"reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" treats a concern as a demonstrated outcome. The fact block says some worry about reduced staff hours; it does not say hours have already been reduced.
The proof list misses the ugly accounting questions: how "restaurant-level margin" is defined, whether capex/depreciation is excluded, sample size, and throughput methodology.
"Without it, both the adoption and the contrarian angle are unsupported" is sloppy. The adoption story needs footprint and timeline proof; the margin range mainly supports the economics story.
